Rolls-Royce Pits Black Against White in Luxury Backgammon Set That Took a Year to Make
9 photos
Photo: Rolls-Royce
With Christmas shopping fever just around the corner, everybody everywhere is scrambling to get ready for what's to come. And I'm not only talking about customers, but the companies that will have something to offer in the months ahead as well. Like, say, British carmaker Rolls-Royce, which seems to have taken a break from making cars this winter and opted to release a backgammon set instead.
That's right, backgammon, the game that has been played by millions (possibly billions), be them aristocracy or addicted gamblers, ever since its early days, some 5,000 years ago, in its presumed point of origin, Mesopotamia.
Now, Rolls-Royce is no stranger to coming up from time to time with products that are anything but cars. You may remember how, in the spring of last year, it came out with a chess set that people with enough money in their bank accounts went nuts over. Probably, the Brits hope this will be the case with the backgammon game as well, especially with Christmas just around the corner.
Described as a playable work of art, the game does come across as being just as luxurious and exquisite as all other things Rolls-Royce. And I'm not talking solely about the materials that were used to make it, but about the way it looks and (probably) feels as well.
Made in-house by the company's Bespoke Collective, the Rolls-Royce backgammon set is made of the same materials and colors the company uses for its cars: ochre, stone, sand (all three meant to remind people of the landscapes of ancient Mesopotamia), aluminum, American walnut, natural grain leather – you name it.
Photo: Rolls-Royce The case itself is crafted from the kind of wood mentioned above, and decorated accordingly, but that's not what makes the board special. As you know, the backgammon case is foldable, and it is at the hinge that Rolls-Royce went nuts.
As a mechanism you'll see nowhere else, made from a solid billet of aluminum, hand-polished and then anodized, it is at the same time both functional and aesthetic. That's because the carmaker designed it in such a way as to rotate open while the central spine counter-rotates to bring into the spotlight the playing pieces and the crafted board.
Because this is a Rolls-Royce creation we're talking about, there is a Spirit of Ecstasy on deck, mounted to the said hinge in such a way that it orients itself regardless of the board's position. Kind of like the self-levelling wheel caps of the real Rolls cars usually do.
The central spine of the case is also where the precision dice, doubling die, and a pair of dice shakers are placed, as is the removable plinth where captured counters can be stored during the game.
Photo: Rolls-Royce When it comes to the playing surface itself, Rolls book-matched it at 55 degrees, just as it happens when it comes to the veneer application in car interiors. The materials used for it include open-pore royal walnut and smoked eucalyptus, among others.
The stones of the game, meaning the actual playing pieces, are made of an undisclosed composite with bauxite ore infusion, and come in Deep Night Sky black and Antarctica white, one color for each player.
Rolls seems to take great pride in the way the anodized aluminum doubling die has been designed, with its shape inspired by the honeycomb structures found in nature, but also the shape of nuts and bolts. The inspiration for this came first and foremost from the company's apiaries in Germany, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, and Qatar .
The final piece of this special backgammon set, the dice shakers, are made of machined aluminum as well, and finished to match the hinge. The bases are made of leather to smooth out the sound of the throw. As a final touch, the Spirit of Ecstasy is engraved beneath.
Photo: Rolls-Royce The reason why this backgammon set exists is not some wacky idea someone over at Rolls-Royce had, but the fact that this game has been tied to the carmaker before: back in 1938, for instance, a Wraith was commissioned with such a thing, built into the rear passenger compartment.
This time, it stands alone and can be purchased by anyone. Ok, maybe not anyone, but definitely the owners of Rolls-Royce cars. Although the company makes no mention of pricing, there is chatter of one such backgammon set selling for around $50,000, which accounts for the displayed level of luxury and takes into account the fact that it took about one year to develop.
Still, that's not nearly as steep as the most expensive backgammon set ever, the $5 million Charles Hollander, or the Geoffrey Parker super-enriched board ($387,000).
Offered at tournament size, the game is not yet listed online (unlike the chess set), but the British company says customers can already ask for one in showrooms and private offices.
